-- $\mu$ - population mean

-- $\sigma$ - population standard deviation

## Last time 

Probability distribution vs sampling distribution 

A probability distribution describes the likelihood of all possible outcomes for a single random variable.

A sampling distribution describes the distribution of a statistic. 

## Question 

Read these as sentences. Which one corresponds to a sampling distribution vs a probability distribution?

$\bar{x} \sim N(\mu, \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}})$

$x \sim N(\mu, \sigma)$

## test-statistic 

Calculate our test statistic using the following formula.

$$t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}}$$

## test-statistic{.smaller}

$$t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}}$$

$$t = \frac{2035 - 2000}{\frac{150}{\sqrt{50}}}$$

$$t = \frac{35}{\frac{150}{7.07107}}$$

$$t = \frac{35}{21.2132}$$

$$t \approx 1.65$$


How do we interpret this number?

## test-statistic 

$$t \approx 1.65$$

2035 $(\bar{x})$ is 1.65 standard errors away from the null value 2000!

## test-statistic 

$$t \approx 1.65$$

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(ggplot2)

# Define parameters for a standard normal distribution
mu <- 0
sigma <- 1

# Generate x values and corresponding normal density values
x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 1000)
df <- data.frame(
  x = x,
  y = dnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
)

# Plot the Empirical Rule (68-95-99.7 Rule)
ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  # Highlight Area 3: Within 3 SDs (99.7%)
  geom_area(data = subset(df, x >= -3 & x <= 3), fill = "#D6EAF8", alpha = 0.8) +
  # Highlight Area 2: Within 2 SDs (95%)
  geom_area(data = subset(df, x >= -2 & x <= 2), fill = "#85C1E9", alpha = 0.8) +
  # Highlight Area 1: Within 1 SD (68%)
  geom_area(data = subset(df, x >= -1 & x <= 1), fill = "#3498DB", alpha = 0.8) +
  
  # Draw standard deviation vertical lines
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3), 
             linetype = "dashed", color = "gray30", alpha = 0.7) +
  
  # Draw normal distribution curve
  geom_line(color = "#1B4F72", size = 1.2) +
  
  # Add percentage annotations
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.20, label = "68%", color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 6) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = 0.08, label = "13.5%", color = "gray20", fontface = "bold", size = 4.5) +
  annotate("text", x = -1.5, y = 0.08, label = "13.5%", color = "gray20", fontface = "bold", size = 4.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.5, y = 0.02, label = "2.35%", color = "gray20", fontface = "bold", size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = -2.5, y = 0.02, label = "2.35%", color = "gray20", fontface = "bold", size = 3.5) +
  
  # Label x-axis ticks using Greek standard deviation symbols
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = -3:3,
    labels = c(expression(mu - 3*sigma), expression(mu - 2*sigma), expression(mu - sigma), 
               expression(mu), 
               expression(mu + sigma), expression(mu + 2*sigma), expression(mu + 3*sigma))
  ) +
  
  # Titles and Styling
  labs(
    title = "The Empirical Rule (68-95-99.7 Rule)",
    subtitle = "Percentage of data falling within 1, 2, and 3 standard deviations of the mean",
    x = "Standard Deviations from the Mean",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, color = "gray30"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank()
  )
```

But there is one problem...... this is a rule for a standard normal distribution.... 

... and we don't have that...

## t-distribution 

[t-distribution]

What is a degree of freedom? 

What t-distribution are we using? 

## Degrees of freedom 

The Wardrobe Analogy

Imagine you have 7 different shirts to wear over a 7-day week. On Monday, you have 7 choices. On Tuesday, 6 choices. By the time Sunday rolls around, you only have 1 shirt left. You have no choice on Sunday—your decision was perfectly determined by the previous 6 days. You had 6 days of true flexibility, meaning your degrees of freedom are 6.

## Degrees of freedom 

Note: We need degrees of freedom because in a single mean test, we also have to use data to estimate $s$ for the standard error. In a single proportion test, the standard error is entirely estimated using our statistic $\hat{p}$. We will re-visit this when we review single proportion.  

How many **independent pieces of information you have** 

If you have $\bar{x}$ and n = 50.... the 50th observation is "locked" into whatever the exact number makes the mean equal to $\bar{x}$ (2035). 

We are working with 49 degrees of freedom!

$t_{49}$

## Complete the story 

Because our statistic follows a $t_{49}$, it is *essentially* the same shape as a normal distribution. Because our test statistic is < 2, our p-value is going to be relatively large. Let's calculate it. 

## p-value 

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(ggplot2)

# Parameters
df_val <- 49
t_stat <- 1.65
p_val_two_tail <- 2 * (1 - pt(t_stat, df = df_val)) # ~ 0.1053

# Generate curve data
x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 1000)
df_plot <- data.frame(
  x = x,
  y = dt(x, df = df_val)
)

ggplot(df_plot, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  # Curve
  geom_line(color = "#1F2937", size = 1) +
  
  # Right tail shading (t >= 1.65)
  geom_area(
    data = subset(df_plot, x >= t_stat),
    fill = "#EF4444", alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  
  # Left tail shading (t <= -1.65)
  geom_area(
    data = subset(df_plot, x <= -t_stat),
    fill = "#EF4444", alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  
  # Vertical test statistic lines
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-t_stat, t_stat), linetype = "dashed", color = "#DC2626", size = 0.8) +
  
  # Annotations for tails
  annotate("text", x = 2.3, y = 0.08, 
           label = paste0("p/2 = ", round(p_val_two_tail / 2, 4)), 
           color = "#B91C1C", fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = -2.3, y = 0.08, 
           label = paste0("p/2 = ", round(p_val_two_tail / 2, 4)), 
           color = "#B91C1C", fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  
  # Custom x-axis breaks
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(-3, -t_stat, -1, 0, 1, t_stat, 3),
    labels = c("-3", "-1.65", "-1", "0", "1", "1.65", "3")
  ) +
  
  # Title and Axis Labels
  labs(
    title = "Two-Tailed p-Value Visualization",
    subtitle = paste0("Student's t-Distribution (df = ", df_val, ", t = ±", t_stat, ")"),
    x = "t-statistic",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, color = "gray40"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank()
  )
```


The probability of observing our statistic, or something more extreme, given the null hypothesis is true.

## Confidence Intervals

A health researcher wants to test whether college students at a local university drink a different amount of water daily compared to the national average. Health guidelines estimate that the national average daily water intake for young adults is 2000 mL.

The researcher selects a simple random sample of $n = 50$ students from the campus library and records their daily water consumption in milliliters (mL). You want to investigate if students at this particular college are different than the national average. Assume that $\bar{x}$ = 2035mL, and $s$ = 150mL

How could we change this question if I wanted to make a confidence interval instead of performing a hypothesis test? 

## Confidence Intervals 

**estimate** 

## Confidence Intervals 

A health researcher wants to test whether college students at a local university drink a different amount of water daily compared to the national average. Health guidelines estimate that the national average daily water intake for young adults is 2000 mL.

The researcher selects a simple random sample of $n = 50$ students from the campus library and records their daily water consumption in milliliters (mL). We want to **estimate** the population mean water consumption for these students on campus. 


## Confidence Interval 

You may use 2.01 for $t^*$. Calculate a 95% confidence interval using the formula below. 

$$\bar{x} \pm t^* \cdot \left( \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \right)$$

## Confidence Interval 

$$\bar{x} \pm t^* \cdot \left( \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \right)$$

$$2035 \pm 2.010 \cdot \left( \frac{150}{\sqrt{50}} \right)$$

$$2035 \pm 2.010 \cdot (21.2132)$$

$$2035 \pm 42.64$$

$$(1992.36\text{ mL},\ 2077.64\text{ mL})$$

how do we interpret this? 


# Questions?

A health researcher wants to see if more than half of college students are drinking water. In a sample size of $n = 50$, the researcher recorded that 35 students drink more than 1 bottle of water a day.

What's different than before?

What's the null and alternative hypothesis?

What type of test are we doing?

## Null and alternative

$Ho: \pi = .5$

$Ha: \pi > .5$

We are going to conduct a z-test, because our response variable is categorical! 

## t vs z-test{.smaller} 

$${SE(\bar{x})} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$

$$\text{Sample Standard Deviation } (s) = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}}$$

vs

$$SE({\hat{p})} = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}$$ 

$${SE(p_o)} = \sqrt{\frac{p_0(1 - p_0)}{n}}$$

Because we know the standard error when we calculate our statistic $\hat{p}$, we are justified to do a z-test and a standard normal distribution. 

## Other formulas 

$$z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{\frac{p_0(1 - p_0)}{n}}}$$


$$\hat{p} \pm z^* \cdot \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}}$$

## Assumptions 

Hypothesis test: 

$$n p_0 \ge 10 \quad \text{and} \quad n (1 - p_0) \ge 10$$


Confidence interval: 

$$n \hat{p} \ge 10 \quad \text{and} \quad n (1 - \hat{p}) \ge 10$$

## z-statistic{.smaller} 

$$z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{\frac{p_0(1 - p_0)}{n}}}$$

$$z = \frac{0.70 - 0.50}{\sqrt{\frac{0.50(1 - 0.50)}{50}}}$$

$$z = \frac{0.20}{\sqrt{\frac{0.25}{50}}}$$

$$z = \frac{0.20}{\sqrt{0.005}}$$

$$z = \frac{0.20}{0.07071}$$

$$z \approx 2.83$$

Draw out how the p-value would be calculated. 

##

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(ggplot2)

# Parameters
z_stat <- 2.83
p_value <- 1 - pnorm(z_stat) # ~ 0.0023

# Generate standard normal curve data
x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 1000)
df_plot <- data.frame(
  x = x,
  y = dnorm(x)
)

ggplot(df_plot, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  # Standard normal curve
  geom_line(color = "#1F2937", size = 1) +
  
  # Right tail shading (z >= 2.83)
  geom_area(
    data = subset(df_plot, x >= z_stat),
    fill = "#EF4444", alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  
  # Vertical line for test statistic
  geom_vline(xintercept = z_stat, linetype = "dashed", color = "#DC2626", size = 0.9) +
  
  # Pointer arrow & annotation for the shaded right tail
  annotate("segment", x = 3.4, xend = 3.0, y = 0.08, yend = 0.01,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm")), color = "#B91C1C", size = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 3.4, y = 0.10, 
           label = paste0("Right-Tail Area\n(p-value = ", round(p_value, 4), ")"), 
           color = "#B91C1C", fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  
  # Custom x-axis breaks
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, z_stat, 4),
    labels = c("-3", "-2", "-1", "0", "1", "2", "2.83", "4")
  ) +
  
  # Titles & Labels
  labs(
    title = "Right-Tailed p-Value Visualization (z-Test)",
    subtitle = "Standard Normal Distribution (Z)",
    x = "z-score",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, color = "gray40"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank()
  )
```

## Confidence interval 

$$\hat{p} \pm z^* \cdot \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}}$$

## Confidence interval{.smaller} 

$$\hat{p} \pm z^* \cdot \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}}$$

$$0.70 \pm 1.96 \cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.70(1 - 0.70)}{50}}$$

$$0.70 \pm 1.96 \cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.70(0.30)}{50}}$$

$$0.70 \pm 1.96 \cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.21}{50}}$$

$$0.70 \pm 1.96 \cdot \sqrt{0.0042}$$

$$0.70 \pm 1.96 \cdot (0.06481)$$

$$0.70 \pm 0.1270$$

$$(0.5730,\ 0.8270) \quad \text{or} \quad (57.30\%,\ 82.70\%)$$
